summary: Defines management objects (a MIB module) for packet sampling. It extends the IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB module so that IPFIX implementations that use Packet Sampling (PSAMP) techniques can be configured and monitored via network management protocols. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Counting every car on a highway is hard, so sometimes you count only some. This memo provides a standard set of dials to control and read how a device picks those samples.

questions: how to configure packet sampling with snmp
which packet sampling methods does the psamp mib cover
what hash functions does psamp support
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let you read which packet sampling and filtering methods a device uses, and with what settings.

tldr.problem: Devices that export IPFIX data may pick only some packets to measure, using sampling and filtering. Operators had no standard SNMP objects to ask which selection methods are active and how they are set.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6727 defines the PSAMP-MIB module, which adds six packet selector function subtrees under the IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB. Each has an availability object and, where it has parameters, a table of parameter sets.
tldr.outcome: The module is read-only and monitoring-only. It is a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed in the metadata.

today: RFC 6727 is a Proposed Standard from October 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the PSAMP MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 6727 defines the PSAMP-MIB module, a Management Information Base (MIB) module for devices that perform packet selection by Sampling and Filtering as described in RFC 5475. It follows the packet sampling framework of RFC 5474 and extends the IPFIX-MIB and IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB modules from RFC 6615.

Because the IPFIX MIB module is only for monitoring, the same holds for this module. It reports which packet selection functions are applied and their parameters. The objects follow the PSAMP information model in RFC 5477. The work started in the Packet Sampling (PSAMP) working group and moved to the IPFIX working group when the PSAMP group concluded.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can choose to look at only some of the traffic. This memo gives a standard way to ask the router which choosing rules it is using.

sections.title: How It Plugs Into the IPFIX Selector MIB
sections.content:
The IPFIX-MIB has the idea of a packet Selection Process that contains a set of Selector function instances. The ipfixSelectionProcessTable names each Selector function instance with an OID that points to an object describing it. A simple function without parameters has just one extra object saying whether it is available. A function with parameters has a subtree holding an availability object and a table with one column per parameter. Each row is one combination of parameter values.

The object ipfixSelectorFunctions is the root for these descriptions. In RFC 6615 it holds only ipfixFuncSelectAll, a trivial function that selects every packet and has no parameters. The PSAMP MIB module registers six more top-level OIDs beneath it, one for each packet Selector function that has parameters. IANA maintains these top-level OIDs.

The module imports two data types from other MIB modules: Unsigned64TC from the APPLICATION-MIB (RFC 2564) and Float64TC from the FLOAT-TC-MIB (RFC 6340). They are not part of the base SMIv2 but are needed to match the Information Elements defined in RFC 5477.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a big filing cabinet for measurement rules, with one drawer that says take every packet. This memo adds six new drawers for the other rules.

sections.title: The Six Selector Functions
sections.content:
The module numbers the new functions from 2, because index 1 is already ipfixFuncSelectAll. Four of them are Sampling methods:

  • Systematic count-based Sampling (psampSampCountBased, 2) has an Interval and a Space parameter.
  • Systematic time-based Sampling (psampSampTimeBased, 3) has the same two parameters, but they hold time values instead of packet counts.
  • Random n-out-of-N Sampling (psampSampRandOutOfN, 4) has a Size and a Population parameter.
  • Uniform probabilistic Sampling (psampSampUniProb, 5) has a single Probability parameter.

Two are Filtering methods: property match Filtering (psampFiltPropMatch, 6) and hash-based Filtering (psampFiltHash, 7). Each Sampling function has an availability object plus a parameter set table. The meaning of the functions is defined in RFC 5475, not here.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six ways to pick packets, like taking every tenth one, picking at random, or rolling a die for each one. Each way has its own little settings page.

sections.title: Property Match and Hash Filtering
sections.content:
Property match Filtering has a broad variety of possible parameters, but RFC 5477 lists no agreed ones. The subtree therefore contains only an availability object, psampFiltPropMatchAvail, and the parameters cannot be retrieved through this MIB module.

Hash-based Filtering is richer. The object psampFiltHashFunction is an enumeration naming the hash: crc32 (the CRC-32 function from RFC 1141), ipsx and bob (both described in RFC 5475, Appendix A). The common parameter set has 7 parameters: an initializer value, an IP payload offset, an IP payload size, the minimum and maximum of the selected range, and the minimum and maximum of the output range. Further parameters depend on the chosen hash and are not specified in this module.
sections.plainLanguage: Hash filtering is like giving every packet a number and keeping only those in a chosen range. The settings tell you which numbering method and which range.

sections.title: Conformance and Groups
sections.content:
The compliance statement says that implementing all objects is optional and depends on whether the equipment implements the matching functionality. The module defines one object group per function. If a device implements, say, count-based Sampling, then the objects in that function's group must be implemented. The same rule applies to time-based, random n-out-of-N, uniform probabilistic, property match and hash Filtering.

The module itself is placed at { mib-2 212 }. Every object it defines is read-only, which fits its monitoring-only role.
sections.plainLanguage: A device only has to fill in the settings pages for the picking methods it actually has.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this module has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, so a correctly implemented module gives an intruder no way to alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

Reading is still a concern. All tables may be sensitive in some environments, because their objects may reveal information about the network infrastructure and device configuration. The RFC says to control even GET and NOTIFY access, and possibly to encrypt the values on the wire. It RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The dials can only be read, not turned, but even reading them could tell a snoop about your network, so keep the window locked.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The module uses the IANA-assigned OBJECT IDENTIFIER psampMIB { mib-2 212 } recorded in the SMI Numbers registry. IANA also registered the six function OIDs in the IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB Functions sub-registry, following the procedures in RFC 6615.

They are 2 psampSampCountBased, 3 psampSampTimeBased, 4 psampSampRandOutOfN, 5 psampSampUniProb, 6 psampFiltPropMatch and 7 psampFiltHash.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers got six new entries so nobody else uses the same ones.
